items.abstract: <jats:p>Advancing Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF), particularly Fast Ignition and Shock Ignition, requires a deeper understanding of laser–plasma interactions in extreme regimes that remain difficult to access at large-scale ICF facilities. Long-wave infrared (LWIR) lasers provide a powerful approach, leveraging favorable wavelength scaling to access relativistic plasma physics, enable efficient laser beam channeling, and enhance the generation of hot electrons and energetic ions at significantly reduced laser intensity and plasma density. This capability allows laboratory-scale experiments to reproduce ICF-relevant conditions with improved diagnostic access and greater physical transparency. The Brookhaven National Laboratory Accelerator Test Facility offers a unique platform for such studies, combining a multi-terawatt LWIR laser with synchronized optical diagnostics and accelerator-based probes. This capability enables systematic investigation and optimization of key plasma processes governing ICF performance, thereby supporting the development of practical fusion energy systems.</jats:p>
title: Long wave infrared laser platform for plasma studies relevant to inertial fusion

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Plasma cathodes often exhibit a bi-modal current–voltage behavior whose physical origin remains unclear, where a low voltage, low current regime transitions to a higher current, high voltage regime at some transition point. Here, two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations using EDIPIC-2D are used to study an argon electron-cyclotron-resonance plasma cathode with an extracting anode, with the goal of identifying the kinetic mechanism connecting this transition point to the formation of a confined orifice plasma. The simulations reveal two self-consistent regimes: a low-current, diffusion dominated state in which the supply of electrons to the orifice is limited, and a high-current state characterized by a dense orifice plasma separated from the prescribed discharge plasma by a weak electrostatic double layer. In the latter regime, the double layer sustains intense localized ionization by accelerating source electrons while regulating particle exchange across the interface. Ion-acoustic wave activity is observed, and a low-Mach-number ion-acoustic shock forms within the double-layer region that produces a pronounced reversal in axial ion current density immediately below this interface. Time-resolved diagnostics reveal the formation mechanism for this orifice plasma that culminates in the coupling of the source, orifice, and plume regions. These results reveal a kinetic, time-dependent mechanism for the bi-modal transition in plasma cathodes and identify electron supply, plume-ionization seeding, and double-layer-shock dynamics as key elements governing access to the high-current regime.</jats:p>
title: A kinetic simulation of orifice plasma formation in plasma cathodes

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To achieve stable single-longitudinal-mode (SLM) operation in an erbium-doped fiber (EDF) configuration, a compound-fiber-ring design can be proposed and systematically investigated. In this work, we introduce an octuple-ring design within the fiber laser cavity to achieve stable SLM output and to realize a wide and tunable wavelength bandwidth across the L-band operation range. The demonstrated octuple-ring EDF laser architecture induces a mode-filtering effect that effectively mitigates thick multi-longitudinal-mode oscillations via the Vernier effect. Based on the designed L-band fiber laser, a wavelength tuning range of 1568.0–1612.0 nm and a linewidth spanning from 312.5–625 Hz are achieved. Furthermore, the output power, optical signal-to-noise ratio (OSNR), and the stability of both power and wavelength are characterized and discussed.</jats:p>
title: Adjustable L-band erbium fiber laser by utilizing compound-ring scheme for single-frequency output

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    To evaluate weak-echo angle retrieval for space-target active laser sensing under strong background, we develop a photon-counting model integrating a vortex-phase-encoded wide-angle metalens (WAM) with a multi-pixel photon counter (MPPC). The WAM maps the incidence angle onto an annular focal spot, while an adaptive pipeline performs full-area response acquisition, coarse centroid estimation, pre-aperture-assisted annular photon selection, multi-response centroid refinement, and angle retrieval. The system model couples laser propagation, Lambertian target reflection, telescope collection, WAM focusing, MPPC parasitic effects, and four-electrode readout. For an idealized 100 km link at zenith and azimuth angles of 30° and 180°, respectively, simulations predict zenith and azimuth errors of 0.0305° and 0.0201°, a detection probability of 99.981%, and a false-alarm probability of 0.0131%. The estimated annular center meets the 0.5
                    <jats:italic>μ</jats:italic>
                    m convergence criterion after four iterations. Without prior knowledge of the true spot center, the adaptive method approaches ideal fixed-annulus selection and markedly outperforms full-surface MPPC integration. This model provides a framework for evaluating and optimizing wide-field photon-counting angle retrieval under weak-echo and strong-background conditions.
                  </jats:p>
title: Model-predicted weak-echo angle retrieval for space-target active laser sensing based on a vortex-phase-encoded wide-angle metalens and multi-pixel photon counter

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum nonlocality, encompassing entanglement, EPR steering, and Bell nonlocality, is a core resource in quantum information science. However, in the literature, these important quantum properties are identified with the non-existence of discrete convex decomposition (D-model) or continuous probabilistic integral representation (C-model), where C- model refers to an integral representation over an arbitrary probability space, which may include atomic measures. This work establishes the equivalences between the C-model and D-model for bipartite separability, EPR unsteerability, and Bell locality in finite-dimensional systems. All proofs are based on an integral mean-value lemma for bounded measurable vector-valued functions on a probability space, which is built upon the Hahn–Banach separation theorem and Carathéodory’s convex hull theorem. This single technical lemma serves as a common tool to convert Bochner integral representations of continuous models into finite convex combinations. Consequently, in a finite dimensional bipartite system, C-separability, C-unsteerability, and C-Bell-locality are equivalent to D-separability, D-unsteerability, and D-Bell-locality, respectively.</jats:p>
title: Equivalence between continuous and discrete models in quantum nonlocality theory

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Time-to-collision (TTC) is widely used in autonomous-driving safety evaluation. However, TTC and many of its extensions quantify risk using one-dimensional closing models, which may limit risk discrimination and misrepresent how risk evolves over time. We introduce evasive acceleration (EA), a physically interpretable two-dimensional (2D) framework for risk quantification. Considering all possible directions of relative acceleration, EA quantifies risk through the minimum magnitude of a constant 2D relative-acceleration vector required to render the extrapolated interaction collision-free. Across five open datasets and 630 reconstructed crash trajectories, EA provides earlier precrash warnings than all six baselines at matched noncrash percentile thresholds, with median lead times up to 2.0 s longer than TTC’s. EA also provides stronger discrimination of eventual collision outcomes than the primary baselines and increases time-averaged retained predictive information about whether a crash occurs by 33.5–270.3% over the compared baselines. Across the evaluated EA–baseline pairs, adding EA yields 5.2–46.8 times as much time-averaged incremental predictive information as adding the corresponding baseline to EA, indicating greater predictive value beyond these baselines. These findings support 2D collision-avoidance demand as a physically interpretable basis for collision-risk quantification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Driving risk emerges from the required two-dimensional joint evasive acceleration

items.abstract: <jats:p>Configuring a diagnostic before the next shot is an instrumentation problem that grows in importance as high-repetition-rate laser-plasma platforms scale from tens of shots to thousands. In the present campaign, a gated intensified optical camera required shot-to-shot retuning as peak image brightness varied with chamber pressure, laser energy, focus conditions, and target state. Static settings produced under-exposed or over-driven images, while manual tuning consumed shots and reduced measurement efficiency. We treat this problem as machine-learning-guided pre-shot diagnostic configuration using a hybrid framework: archived images and machine variables are reduced to a compact descriptor state, a neural-network surrogate is trained to predict that state from operating conditions and detector settings, and Bayesian optimization inverts the surrogate to recommend executable settings before each shot. On a 1 Hz multi-joule platform, the measured peak signal tracked requested targets from 1000 to 4500 counts with a correlation of 0.92 and a mean absolute error of 15%. These results demonstrate that campaign data can train practical empirical models supporting pre-shot diagnostic configuration for enhanced data quality and experimental efficiency in comparable laser-plasma campaigns.</jats:p>
title: Machine-learning-guided pre-shot diagnostic configuration for high-repetition-rate laser-plasma experiments

<jats:sec id="st1">
                    <jats:title>Introduction:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Androgenic/Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) typically involves a receding hairline, hair loss on the crown, or both. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is an effective autologous blood product with a large concentration of platelets used for treatment of AGA. Microneedling, a minimally invasive procedure with fine needles, stimulates stem cells and growth factors. We aim to study the efficacy and safety of PRP with microneedling vs PRP in the treatment of AGA</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st2">
                    <jats:title>Material and Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      54 AGA patients separated into 2 groups of 27 each were enrolled. After ethical clearance, Group 1 underwent three sessions of PRP therapy, while Group 2 underwent PRP in combination with 1-mm dermaroller microneedling. The patient’s hair growth and density were assessed using a seven-point scale, and physicians evaluated hair growth from baseline photos using the same scale. Statistical analysis was performed using descriptive and inferential methods, with the Chi-square test applied, and a
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      value <0.05 considered statistically significant.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st3">
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Both groups showed statistically significant improvement on both subjective and objective assessments. On subjective assessment, mild-to-moderate improvement was observed in 74.1% of the PRP group and 77.8% of the PRP+MN group (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      =0.0001 for both). On objective assessment, mild-to-moderate improvement was seen in 88.9% of the PRP group and 77.8% of the PRP+MN group (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.0001 for both), with minimal non-responders or worsening in either group. Small sample size, Attrition to follow-up, lack of long-term (>6months) follow-up, lack of trichoscopic evaluation were the limitations of the study.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="st4">
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The addition of microneedling to PRP did not result in a statistically significant difference (Subjective
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      =0.98, Objective
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      =0.37), although patients with PRP+MN experienced better results.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Comparison of microneedling with platelet rich plasma therapy versus platelet rich plasma therapy in patients of androgenic alopecia: A prospective study

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Reconfigurable metasurfaces provide a versatile platform for dynamically manipulating optical wavefronts, enabling emerging applications in holography, information processing, and optical encryption. However, existing phase‐change metasurface holograms predominantly exploit binary transitions between amorphous and crystalline phases, which severely restrict the attainable information capacity. Here we present a multilevel phase‐change metasurface architecture that leverages multiple intermediate crystallization states to encode substantially more holographic channels. We further introduce a cascaded metasurface configuration, where propagation‐assisted cooperative modulation creates an additional encoding dimension while mitigating inter‐channel crosstalk. By integrating the device physics into an end‐to‐end differentiable optimization framework, the cascaded structure is jointly optimized for dynamic multichannel holographic reconstruction. Numerical demonstrations validate that distinct combinations of crystallization states across the cascaded metasurfaces can selectively reconstruct multiple holographic images with high fidelity. This scalable strategy expands the information capacity of programmable metasurface holography and opens new opportunities for high‐density optical encryption, multidimensional information storage, and programmable wavefront engineering.</jats:p>
title: Reconfigurable Multi‐Channel Holography Based on Multi‐Level Phase‐Change Metasurfaces

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Using multimode fiber (MMF) as an architype complex optical medium, we introduce Dispersion‐Steered Modes (DSMs) for dynamic spatio‐spectral wave control. Unlike previous approaches that suppress modal dispersion to maintain static phase‐locking, DSMs actively transform the intrinsic dispersion into a synthetic transverse momentum. By utilizing spatio‐spectral operators to construct a generalized eigenvalue equation, we establish a deterministic mapping between spectral detuning and spatial translation. Specifically, we analyze the complex spatial velocity (the eigenvalue of the equation) and elucidate the physical meaning of its real and imaginary parts: the former governs spatial translation, and the latter degrades mode field stability. To obtain optimal modes, we establish a dual‐criterion selection mechanism based on the mean‐delay approximation and tailored inter‐mode coupling to synthesize robust DSMs that achieve dynamic steering with minimal spatial distortion. With experimental verification showing continuous translation of the focusing spot across a 1 THz bandwidth and spatial fidelity maintained above 0.8, this operator‐driven approach provides a framework for dynamic light manipulation in complex scattering environments.</jats:p>
title: Translational Steering With Multimodal Dispersion

items.abstract: <jats:p>Bulky fan arrays and room-scale airflow systems have shown that wind can enhance presence in Virtual Reality (VR), but they are difficult to deploy and do not readily support head-worn, spatially coherent cues. We present AirHook, a lightweight ear-hook wind interface that delivers omnidirectional airflow around the periauricular region without interfering with a head-mounted display. AirHook renders spatial, dynamic 3D wind cues by activating a compact nozzle array with a head-contingent airflow rendering algorithm, enabling intermediate directions beyond discrete nozzle orientations. We evaluate AirHook in three studies: two perceptual studies respectively characterizing 3D direction recognition across stimulus durations and a 36° directional-resolution benchmark, and a VR study comparing No Wind, Non-directional Wind, and Multi-directional Wind, combining questionnaires and interviews. Results show that multi-directional wind provides additional experiential benefits beyond non-directional airflow and yields practical design implications for ear-based wind feedback.</jats:p>
title: AirHook: Simulating Multi-directional Wind Around Ears to Enhance Presence in VR

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Photon blockade is of critical importance for realizing single‐photon emitters and for the quantum simulation of interacting systems with light. Through destructive quantum interference, strong photon blockade in a cavity system can be observed even in the common weak‐coupling (weak‐nonlinearity) regime. However, previous protocols to realize such unconventional photon blockade require fine‐tuning of system parameters and can only operate within particular time windows. Leveraging dark‐state physics, we report in this work a mechanism for robust photon blockade operating continuously without fine‐tuning. Specifically, we consider a system consisting of a two‐level atom weakly coupled to an optical cavity supporting two coupled modes. Under a weak on‐resonance probe field, quantum interference creates single‐ and double‐excitation dark states, and the coupling strength between these two types of dark states is drastically reduced by quantum destructive interference. The dominating single‐excitation dark state, resonantly coupled with the probe field, then leads to a photon blockade mechanism that is robust against cavity parameter variations and allows continuous‐time operations of photon blockade. We discuss possible applications of such dark‐state‐mediated photon blockade in the realization of a narrow‐bandwidth single‐photon source.</jats:p>
title: Robust Interference‐Induced Photon Blockade Mediated by Dark States

items.abstract: <jats:p>This article investigates the influence of laser processing parameters on the hardness of the surface layer structural carbon steel grade 45 (GOST 1050) and chromium-alloyed steel grade 40Kh (GOST 4543). The study examines laser hardening as a surface heat-treatment method that can increase the hardness and wear resistance of machine components while maintaining the toughness of their cores. Experimental investigations were conducted using a MiniMarker-2 precision laser marking system on specimens made of steels 45 and steel 40Kh. The effects of laser power density and other technological parameters, including processing speed and pulse frequency, on the hardness of the treated surface were investigated. Hardness was measured using the Rockwell method. The experimental results demonstrated that changes in laser power density significantly affect the hardness of the investigated steels. In the initial range of the selected processing parameters, an increase in laser power was accompanied by a decrease in hardness, indicating the need to adjust the laser processing conditions. Based on the experimental findings, possible directions for further optimisation of the laser processing parameters were identified, including adjustments to pulse frequency, processing speed and hatch spacing. The results may be used in developing laser-hardening technologies for machine parts and mechanical components.</jats:p>
title: THE EFFECT OF LASER PROCESSING PARAMETERS ON THE HARDNESS OF STEELS

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantum networks play a pivotal role in quantum information science, as they not only provide a secure communication platform for remote access to quantum computers but also serve as the strategic core for achieving large‐scale quantum information processing, forming the foundational infrastructure for the future global‐scale quantum internet. Quantum teleportation, which enables the transmission of unknown quantum states over long distances by employing quantum entanglement together with classical communication, is essential for the distribution of quantum resources in the construction of the global‐scale quantum internet. To realize a global‐scale quantum internet, quantum repeater protocols represent one of the most promising approaches for enabling quantum communication between any nodes. This concise review presents representative experimental demonstrations of quantum teleportation for constructing quantum networks across different physical platforms. Along this trajectory, the review discusses current challenges, open issues, and future perspectives toward a scalable and practical quantum internet.</jats:p>
title: Quantum Teleportation Toward the Quantum Internet: A Concise Review

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Background. Wound healing complications, including graft failure, infection, scarring, and delayed epithelialization, remain challenges in otorhinolaryngology surgery. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) are autologous adjuncts that may enhance tissue repair. The aim of this study is to assess the clinical efficacy and safety of autologous platelet concentrates (PRP and PRF) compared with standard surgery or non-active controls in otorhinolaryngology-head and neck surgery.
Research Method. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, SpringerLink, and Semantic Scholar were searched from inception to May 2026, following PRISMA 2020. English full-text randomized trials and prospective non-randomized comparative studies of platelet concentrates (PRP, PRF, or plasma rich in growth factors) in ear, nose, throat, head, and neck procedures were included; secondary reviews were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, and results were synthesized narratively.
Findings. Sixty-one studies (45 randomized, 16 non-randomized) were included, with low-to-moderate risk of bias. In tympanic membrane repair, graft uptake was 78%–100% with PRP or PRF versus 22.2%-92.5% in controls, with the greatest benefit in large or anterior perforations; infection and otorrhea decreased, but hearing gains were inconsistent. After sinonasal surgery and tonsillectomy, early crusting and pain decreased, but secondary tonsillar hemorrhage and long-term sinonasal outcomes did not improve. Scar quality improved; evidence for fistula, voice, and olfactory outcomes was limited.
Conclusion. PRP and PRF are safe adjuncts, most useful for high-risk graft closure, early mucosal healing, and scar quality. Future research should standardize preparation protocols and evaluate long-term outcomes in high-risk subgroups.</jats:p>
title: PLATELET-RICH PLASMA AND PLATELET-RICH FIBRIN FOR WOUND HEALING IN OTORHINOLARYNGOLOGY: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF CLINICAL OUTCOMES

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents the results of an investigation into the effect of technological parameters of the laser cutting process on the surface quality and condition of the subsurface layer of 10 mm thick S355J2C+N structural steel. The experiments were conducted using a fiber laser cutting machine with oxygen as the process gas. The effects of focus f, feed rate V, and peak power P on the surface roughness parameters Ra, Rq, and Rc were analyzed, considering the cross-sectional position at the top, center, and bottom parts of the cut edge. The selection of these parameters enables a comprehensive assessment of surface roughness by considering both average profile deviations and extreme variations in profile height. In addition, the heat-affected zone (HAZ) width, subsurface microhardness, and microstructural were evaluated. ANOVA and regression models were used to assess the relationships between the process parameters and surface roughness. The results showed that feed rate and peak power, as well as their interaction, had the most significant effects on surface roughness. The highest roughness values occurred in the top zone of the cut edge. The developed regression models for the surface topography parameters exhibited high predictive capability, with coefficients of determination R2 exceeding 86%. Multi-criteria optimization considering Ra, Rq, and Rc simultaneously identified focus f = 0.30 mm, feed rate v = 1.52 m/min, and peak power P = 3600 W as the most favorable process conditions. The analysis of the subsurface layer revealed microstructural changes in the immediate vicinity of the cut edge and an increase in HAZ width with increasing laser power, whereas increasing feed rate reduced the HAZ width. The HAZ width ranged from approximately 320 to 396 µm, while microhardness ranged from approximately 204 to 220 HV0.3.</jats:p>
title: Surface Integrity of Structural Steel After Laser Cutting: Analysis of Surface Roughness and Heat-Affected Zone

items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">In this study, a conical-tipped atmospheric-pressure plasma tube was designed and fabricated to generate atmospheric-pressure plasma for plasma medicine applications. The plasma generated using conical-tipped plasma tube (CT) was compared with that generated using flat-tipped plasma tube (FT), commonly used in literature, in terms of three parameters: plasma composition, antibacterial activity, and anticancer activity. The reactive species generated in plasma were analyzed using optical emission spectroscopy (OES). Antibacterial activity was evaluated using Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) as model bacterial strains. Anticancer activity was assessed using MCF10A, MCF-7, MDA-MB-231 cell lines. According to OES results, CT indicated higher reactive content than FT at same discharge power and frequency. Antibacterial assay results demonstrated that plasma generated by CT exhibited approximately threefold greater antibacterial activity against S. aureus than plasma generated by FT. Against E. coli, plasma generated by CT was approximately six times more effective than that generated by FT and exhibited antibacterial activity over larger surface area. According to anticancer assay results, viability of healthy MCF10A cells remained above 75% following 30 s direct plasma treatment with both plasma sources. In contrast, CT demonstrated greater anticancer efficacy against cancer cell lines, reducing cell viability below 10%.</jats:p>
title: Comparative Analysis of Plasmas Produced by Conical-tipped and Flat-tipped Atmospheric Pressure Plasma Tubes

                  <jats:p>
                    Global longitudinal wave‐3/4 peak structures in the ionosphere and the lower thermosphere have been recognized and investigated over the past two decades. However, the peak structures are uneven and contain pronounced differences in the spheres, and the mechanism remains less investigated. This study analyzed the electron density of Global Ionospheric Specification (GIS) and neutral winds from Ionospheric Connection Explorer (ICON) to investigate the longitudinal unevenness. The new finding is that, over the Asian‐Pacific region, strong eastward winds occurred in the lower thermosphere above 126 km. The eastward winds in the
                    <jats:italic>E</jats:italic>
                    ‐region dynamo can drive eastward plasma drifts in the
                    <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                    region, which can contribute to the formation of the ionospheric peak structures, particularly over the Asian‐Pacific sectors, and further lead to the longitudinal unevenness. The results reveal that the ionospheric electrodynamics is complex at the Asian‐Pacific longitudes, even though the geomagnetic geometry is relatively simple.
                  </jats:p>
title: F ‐Region Plasma Density Modulated by Zonal Wind in Lower Thermosphere Over Asian‐Pacific Region

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Space filling of forests refers to the proportion of three-dimensional (3-D) space occupied by plants. Quantifying the patterns and influencing factors of space filling is important for better understanding biological interactions such as competition and for improving forest function modeling. However, forest space filling is seldom quantified, especially in structurally complex rainforests. Leveraging lightweight terrestrial laser scanning derived 3-D point cloud data, we quantified understory space filling in a 12-ha Amazonian rainforest. Combined with ground census data, we also explored the influencing factors of the understory space filling. We found that the absolute amount of understory space filling was influenced by the choice of voxel size, but its spatial pattern remains highly similar despite changing voxel sizes, following a fractal scaling law for voxel edge lengths ranging from 10 cm to 2 m. The fractal dimensions across all subplots ranged from 2.061 to 2.326. With a voxel edge length of 30 cm, values of understory space filling ranged from 23% to 44% across the 12-ha study region with marked spatial heterogeneity. Higher space filling was associated with higher tree diversity, lower terrain elevation, and wetter topographic conditions. Understory with low light availability exhibited significantly reduced understory space filling. Overall, our study demonstrated the feasibility of using a lightweight terrestrial laser scanner to quantify understory space filling in structurally complex rainforests. The results also highlight the important roles of biotic and abiotic factors in shaping space filling, thereby advancing our understanding of the formation of rainforest 3-D structure.</jats:p>
title: Patterns and influencing factors of understory space filling in a tropical rainforest revealed by terrestrial laser scanning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Bee pollen (BP) is a source of nutrients and bioactive compounds; however, its impact on the plasma lipidome of goats is not well established. Thirty clinically healthy, dry (non-pregnant and non-lactating), crossbred Boer × Spanish does, each two years old, were assigned to either a BP-supplemented group (T-BP; n = 15) or a control group (T-CTL; n = 15). The T-BP group received 10 g BP per day with 50 g commercial feed for 42 days, while the control group received the feed without BP. Lipidomic profiling was conducted on 20 selected goats (10 per treatment), with samples collected at Day −8, Days 21 and 42, and Day 56. Of 80 planned specimens, 78 were included in the laboratory dataset; the complete-case MetaboAnalyst analysis utilized 72 observations from female goats. After interquartile-range filtering, 1722 of 2870 analytical features remained. Principal component analysis indicated overlapping treatment distributions and a consistent pattern across sampling times. Exploratory PERMANOVA analysis yielded R2 = 0.0062 and p = 0.65 for treatment. In ANOVA–simultaneous component analysis, nominal p values were 0.11 for Treatment, less than 0.01 for Time, and 0.89 for the Treatment × Time interaction. Leverage and squared prediction error criteria identified 51 Time-associated and 64 interaction-submodel signals, which represent model contributors rather than confirmed differential lipids. As permutation analyses did not establish valid within-goat inference, these findings do not support treatment-specific longitudinal effects. This study describes temporal plasma lipidomic variation and highlights analytical signals for future confirmation.</jats:p>
title: Longitudinal Plasma Lipidomic Profiles in Goats Receiving Bee Pollen

Los espectros Raman presentaron bandas próximas a 1340, 1580 y 2700 cm⁻¹, asignadas a las bandas D, G y 2D. Las relaciones entre las áreas ajustadas de las bandas D y G fueron 0.962, 0.593 y 0.946 para las muestras P1, P2 y P3, respectivamente. Los difractogramas mostraron señales compatibles con un ordenamiento grafítico limitado y las micrografías revelaron estructuras de apariencia laminar. Los resultados respaldan la formación de materiales carbonosos con características grafíticas y de grafeno multicapa.</jats:p>

                    Approximately 20%–30% of children with primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) develop chronic ITP due to persistent disease courses. Current laboratory indicators exhibit limited predictive accuracy. A prospective cohort of newly diagnosed children with ITP was established. Patients were classified into chronic (n=42) and non-chronic (n=47) groups based on outcomes after a 12-month follow-up, totaling 89 cases. Among them, 12 cases underwent 4D-DIA proteomic screening of plasma differential proteins; 77 cases underwent ELISA validation. Subsequently, univariate analyses of clinical indicators and myeloid cell nuclear differentiation antigen (MNDA) levels were performed to preliminarily screen candidate variables, LASSO regression (λ
                    <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                    se) performed dimension reduction, and Firth penalized logistic regression built a combined predictive model. ROC curves evaluated diagnostic performance; bootstrap resampling (B = 1000) performed internal validation. LASSO identified 6 non-zero coefficient variables: plasma MNDA, absolute lymphocyte count (ALC), mean platelet volume at day 7 (MPV-D7), platelet count at 1 month (PLT-1M), platelet large cell ratio at 1 month (P-LCR-1M), and cystatin C. The Firth model was significant overall (χ
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                     = 56.98, df=6, P&lt;0.001); MNDA, PLT-1M, and cystatin C were independent predictors of chronic ITP. The combined model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.961, corrected AUC of 0.934 (optimism=0.028), and Brier score of 0.08. Single-indicator ROC showed PLT-1M had the highest AUC (0.899); the combined model outperformed all single indicators (all P&lt;0.05). This exploratory model is applicable for reclassifying the risk of progression to chronicity in children with ITP after one month of treatment, offering new insights for personalized follow-up strategies.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background and Objectives: Evidence directly comparing platelet-rich plasma (PRP), ozone therapy, and their combination in hip osteoarthritis is limited. This study evaluated whether longitudinal changes in pain differed among these three treatment groups. Materials and Methods: This retrospective multicenter cohort study included 147 patients treated with ozone, PRP, or PRP + ozone and followed for 12 months. The primary outcome was the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS); secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) and the physical and mental component scores of the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-12). Outcomes were analyzed using a center-adjusted mixed model for repeated measures, with an additional multivariable-adjusted sensitivity analysis. Results: The treatment × time interaction was significant for NRS (Wald χ2 = 62.69, df = 6, p < 0.001). At 3 months, center-adjusted between-group differences in NRS change from baseline favored PRP + ozone over ozone (−1.20 points; 95% CI, −1.68 to −0.72; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and PRP (−0.75 points; 95% CI, −1.23 to −0.28; Holm-adjusted p = 0.010). At 6 and 12 months, both PRP-containing groups showed greater NRS improvement than ozone, while no statistically significant difference between PRP and PRP + ozone was detected. Similar patterns were observed for WOMAC and SF-12 at these later visits. No serious adverse events were recorded. Conclusions: PRP + ozone was associated with greater early pain improvement, whereas both PRP-containing regimens showed greater improvement relative to baseline at 6 and 12 months than ozone alone, despite attenuation of the initial improvement. These observational findings do not establish comparative efficacy or causality.</jats:p>
title: Platelet-Rich Plasma, Ozone, or Both for Hip Osteoarthritis: A Multicenter Comparative Clinical Study over 12 Months

items.abstract: <jats:p>Navigating field research that involves collecting qualitative and quantitative data can be difficult. The added layer of cultural immersion, language barriers, and economic disparities creates additional challenges to what may already be an arduous undertaking. In this article, I reflect on my professional and personal experiences of conducting field research in Chilika Lagoon, India, where I applied an interdisciplinary approach to examining significant fish species for Chilika fishers. Further, I discuss acclimatizing to a field setting and the difficulties I faced in a cross‐cultural research context. These challenges and experiences helped me recognize the importance of community support, adaptability, and willingness to learn when conducting cross‐cultural research. I conclude with insights for future researchers to consider within a new context.</jats:p>
title: Reflections From the Field: Conducting Culturally Immersive Field Research as an Interdisciplinary Researcher

items.abstract: <jats:p>When the number of scattering centers is fixed, allocating limited model capacity to localized strong responses can leave valid low-amplitude responses underrepresented. To address this issue, we propose an image-domain method for extracting extended attributed scattering centers by combining Adaptive Threshold and Resolution-based Clustering (ATRC) with Coverage-Oriented Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (COOMP). Spatially representative candidate centers are first generated. Strong scatterers are then recovered preferentially, and a stage transition governed by the marginal improvement in fit determines the capacity available for subsequent selection. Candidate selection jointly considers correlation with the complex residual, dynamically assessed undercoverage in the linear and logarithmic amplitude domains, and spatial separation. Trial reconstruction, protection of strong-response regions, and local position refinement are subsequently used to obtain a fixed-capacity representation. Complex-valued SAR images in an equivalent spotlight configuration were formed from coherent complex far-field data simulated in CST for a single ship model treated as a perfect electric conductor (PEC). Baseline pipeline comparisons and module ablation experiments were conducted with a fixed number of scattering centers. In the main simulation scenario at K=40, removing the coverage-oriented module for allocating the remaining center budget increased the weak-region complex normalized mean squared error (NMSE) from 0.556 to 0.611 and reduced the strong-region matched energy from 98.851% to 98.845%. On both measured MSTAR samples, the proposed method ranked first among the five methods in structural similarity, image correlation, and support recall. Its target-region complex NMSE was the second highest for the T-72 sample and the highest for the BTR-70 sample. Further validation is needed on a broader range of targets and on measured SAR data from ship scenes.</jats:p>
title: Strong–Weak Scattering Collaborative Attributed Scattering Center Extraction for Spotlight-Equivalent SAR Ship Imagery Under a Fixed Model-Capacity Constraint

items.abstract: <jats:p>Objectives. Nuclear medicine technologists are chronically exposed to ionising radiation, yet the biological effects of chronic low-dose exposure remain poorly understood. This exploratory pilot study investigated DNA and chromosomal damage in technologists as biomarkers of occupational radiation exposure. Methods. DNA double-strand breaks were quantified by γH2AX immunofluorescence in cultured lymphocytes from blood samples of 20 technologists before and after radiotracer administration as well as from age- and sex-matched controls. The frequency of dicentric chromosomes, a well-established marker of radiation damage, was also scored. Participants completed questionnaires on occupational and lifestyle factors. Historical dose records were reviewed and dosimetry practices assessed by observation of dosimeter use. Results. Following routine radiopharmaceutical administration, technologists showed higher background γH2AX foci/cell than controls. Technologists also showed higher dicentric chromosome frequencies than controls while higher frequencies were observed among participants with a family history of cancer. There was a modest difference in the mean γH2AX foci/cell frequency between female and male participants. No significant associations were observed with smoking status and age. Weak correlations were noted with years of employment. Compliance with wearing personal dosimeters was high among technologists. Conclusions. γH2AX foci and dicentric chromosome frequencies were highly variable across groups and higher in nuclear medicine technologists. These findings provide preliminary evidence of differences in biomarkers of DNA and chromosomal damage in occupationally exposed technologists, suggesting that these biomarkers may have potential for detecting biological effects of low-dose occupational radiation exposure. Larger long-term studies are needed to determine whether these differences are related to occupational radiation exposure or to other factors that vary between individuals, and to assess the potential utility of these biomarkers for individualised routine biological monitoring as a supplement to dosimetry monitoring.</jats:p>
title: An Exploratory Study of DNA and Chromosomal Damage in UK Nuclear Medicine Technologists

items.abstract: <jats:p>Decadal climate predictions can inform decision-making in the short to medium term. Here, we conduct a preliminary assessment of the potential skill in predicting surface wind speed and downward solar radiation, which may be useful for planning the development of renewable energy capacity. We use experiments from the Decadal Climate Prediction Project and the Detection and Attribution Model Intercomparison Project to assess skill, and the drivers of skill, at global and regional scales. We find that decadal predictions of surface downward solar radiation are skillful at the global scale and across several large-scale regions. Skill appears to result largely from trends driven by external forcing from greenhouse gases and tropospheric aerosols, and, at the global scale, from naturally occurring volcanic eruptions. Nevertheless, some skill remains even after these signals are removed, suggesting the influence of initialization and the predictability of natural modes of variability. Skill in predicting surface wind speed is lower, but smaller-scale regional signals from forced climate trends may be predictable. The results highlight that decadal predictions from climate models could be useful for planning for renewable energy.</jats:p>
title: Predictability of near-surface wind and solar radiation on decadal time scales

items.abstract: <jats:p>Improvements in cancer treatment have produced a growing population of survivors who are of reproductive age or will reach reproductive age. For many, loss of fertility is among the most consequential late effects of cancer treatment. Radiation therapy can impair fertility through direct gonadal injury and through injury to the uterus or hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This narrative review examines the quantitative radiation biology of male and female reproductive organs and translates it into practical treatment-planning measures. These include dose estimation, field and modality selection, shielding, ovarian or uterine transposition, and documentation of estimated gonadal dose. Established fertility-preservation options are also reviewed, together with pregnancy and offspring safety, uncertainties in dose constraints, and barriers to implementation. The practical conclusion is that fertility preservation should be addressed before treatment begins, with radiation dose to reproductive organs treated as a modifiable planning objective whenever this can be achieved without compromising tumor control.</jats:p>
title: Fertility protection in male and female cancer patients: Emphasis on safe radiation oncology treatment

items.abstract: <jats:p>Reaction time is an important component of judo performance, because athletes must respond rapidly to tactile cues from an opponent while maintaining grip control and balance. Existing assessments rely mainly on visual tasks that may not re&#64258;ect the somatosensory demands of the sport. This study describes the development of a low-cost, portable haptic choice reaction device delivering localized tactile stimuli through judogi-covered grips, and an initial evaluation of its repeatability. Ten physically active adults, including four internationally competitive judoka, completed six simple and choice reaction tasks across two sessions: Deary-Liewald (DL) visual tasks on a laptop, and device-based tasks using visual or haptic prompts. Median reaction times showed the expected simple-to-choice distinction in every modality, and the haptic simple task was the fastest. The haptic choice task produced a test&ndash;retest intraclass correlation coe&#64259;cient, ICC(A,1), of .61 (95% CI [&minus;.02, .89]), similar to .62 (95% CI [.00, .89]) for the DL choice task in the same participants. However, both intervals span poor to good reliability. Typical error was 48 ms for the haptic task and 31 ms for the DL task, giving minimum detectable changes of 133 ms and 86 ms, respectively. Accuracy was lower in the haptic choice task (81.9%) than the DL choice task (92.0%), and within the haptic task it was lower for stimuli delivered to the left grip (69.7%) than the right (91.8%). The originality of this work lies in integrating a grip-based tactile stimulus into a portable reaction time device and in showing that stimulus detection alone is unlikely to explain the haptic choice task&rsquo;s lower precision. The principal limitation of this study is the small, mixed sample, which produced imprecise reliability estimates. These &#64257;ndings provide proof of concept for a judo-oriented haptic reaction time task; the measurement error is too large to monitor individual athletes, and validation in an adequately powered judoka sample is required.</jats:p>
title: Development and initial evaluation of a judo-oriented haptic reaction device: A proof-of-concept reliability study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diagnosis of peanut allergy in children is suggestive from allergic history, with oral peanut challenges being the gold standard. Symptom presentation may vary based on age and development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate age-related differences during in-office peanut oral challenges that may assist paediatricians overseeing challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A retrospective chart review of peanut oral challenges in children with suspected peanut allergy was performed. Data was obtained from in-office challenges using peanut flour 0.5g protein/g (PB2 powder) with incremental doses. Threshold dose of reactions, time to onset of initial and moderate-severe (M-S) symptoms, and symptom type were collected. Comparison of children's peanut specific skin prick test (SPT) and serum IgE results were made in the positive challenge population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chart review was carried out from 2023-6 in younger (0-3 yrs) and older (4-9 yrs). An arbitrary age of 3 years was selected based on paediatric development and verbal ability to report symptoms. Allergic reactions occurred in 8 of 23 (35.78%) infants/toddlers and 9 of 19 (47.37%) older children. In older children, the mean time to initial and M-S symptoms was 60.0±23.1 and 62.9±24.9 minutes, respectively. In contrast, infants/toddlers developed initial and M-S symptoms at 89.6±60.1 and 125.8±46.0 minutes, respectively. Time to first M-S reaction was significantly longer in infants/toddlers than in older children (125.8±46.5 vs 62.9±24.9 minutes; p=0.003). Older children showed symptoms earlier at lower doses (0.033g), whereas infants/toddlers reacted later at higher doses (0.143g). Mean SPT wheal sizes were 10.9±2.8 mm in older children and 8.8±2.5 mm in infants/toddlers (p=0.124), while peanut-specific IgE were 17.1±14.3 kU/L in older children and 26.6±18.1 kU/L in infants/toddlers (p=0.243). Additionally, 45% of symptoms experienced by infant/toddlers were GI-related, while 52% of symptoms in the older children were respiratory-related.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older children’s initial and M-S symptoms occurred almost simultaneously, while infants/toddlers displayed a delay between them. Additionally, infants/toddlers exhibited a significantly longer time to develop M-S symptoms. SPT and IgE results could not predict response time as no significant difference was observed. GI symptoms were more common in younger children; skin symptoms in older children. Overall, these findings suggest that extended post-challenge observation may be necessary in younger age groups to ensure safety during peanut oral challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: 68 Be aware! Early years, later reactions: Differences in reaction timing during peanut oral challenge in children

<jats:p>Single-aperture stellar kinematics jointly constrain the mass distribution, tracer light profile, and velocity anisotropy. Their coupling affects the interpretation of an inferred anisotropy.
We quantify how tracer-profile assumptions and data treatment affect common-anisotropy comparisons and inferred mass-density slopes in a compiled galaxy-scale lens sample.
We analyzed 107 lenses using distinct supernova counterparts, spatial flatness, distance duality, and the full supernova covariance. We compared the individual-slope power-law tracer with Hernquist and Sérsic profiles using measured effective radii. Numerical Jeans solutions, likelihood comparisons, posterior distributions, and controlled recovery experiments quantified the effects of tracer representation.
The power-law fixed-minus-free Bayesian information criterion differences are 6.74 for isotropy and 41.51 for fixed β=0.18, compared with -3.89 and -2.26 for Hernquist and -4.67 and -4.30 for Sérsic n=4. The preference also changes with the Sérsic index. Removing 12 systems with a linearized distance-ratio uncertainty of above 20% reduces the power-law isotropy comparison to 2.51. In isotropic Sérsic n=4 and Hernquist simulations, power-law fits yield Δ _0>6 in 60.0% and 50.0% of realizations, respectively, compared with 0.5% and 1.0% for matched-tracer fits. BIC
The preference for a common free anisotropy parameter depends on the tracer representation and sample composition. Controlled recovery identifies tracer mismatch as one mechanism that can generate this preference within the adopted aperture models. Physical interpretation requires a joint treatment of photometry, distance uncertainties, and kinematic weighting.</jats:p>
title: Anisotropy and tracer-profile assumptions in aperture-based strong-lens dynamics. Conditional inference from supernova distance ratios and unresolved stellar kinematics

items.abstract: <jats:p>Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis (NEH) is an uncommon, benign, self-limiting dermatosis that is primarily observed in acute myeloid leukemia patients receiving chemotherapy. Here, we are reporting a case of nilotinib-induced NEH in a patient with chronic myeloid leukemia. The patient presented with fever, chills, and erythematous edematous plaques with blisters on her forearms, thighs, legs, palms, and soles 10 days following the initiation of nilotinib. Differential diagnoses such as bullous sweet syndrome, autoimmune blistering diseases, and cellulitis were ruled out through histopathological analysis and negative culture results. Skin biopsy showed necrosis of eccrine glands. Nilotinib was stopped, and the patient was treated with systemic steroids. She was subsequently started on dasatinib, which she tolerated well.</jats:p>
title: Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis associated with nilotinib: An adverse cutaneous reaction

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Field-based functional assessment in university sports settings has largely focused on strength, balance, jumping performance and joint range of motion, whereas simple reaction-time performance has received comparatively little attention. This study examined the association between sports-major background and simple reaction time in physically active university students, with sequential adjustment for demographic characteristics, BMI, training exposure and health histories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 263 physically active university students, comprising 132 sports-major students and 131 non-sports-major students who engaged in regular exercise. The primary outcome was log-transformed simple reaction time; raw values in milliseconds and reverse-standardised scores were used as supplementary outcomes. Multivariable linear regression was used to assess the association between sports-major background and reaction time. Models were adjusted for sex, age, body mass index, weekly training duration, years of training, sports injury history in the past 12 months, and low back pain in the past 3 months, using CR2 cluster-robust inference with Satterthwaite correction across nine clusters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Raw simple reaction time was shorter in the sports-major group than in the non-sports-major group (269.4 ± 37.2 ms vs. 297.4 ± 49.9 ms), with a mean difference of − 28.0 ms (95% confidence interval [CI], − 38.7 to − 17.3; P < 0.001). In the fully adjusted model, sports-major background remained associated with shorter log-transformed simple reaction time (β = −0.128; 95% CI, − 0.193 to − 0.063; P = 0.002), corresponding to an approximately 12.0% shorter reaction time. Wild cluster bootstrap inference supported the association (95% CI, − 0.200 to − 0.072; P = 0.002), and all leave-one-cluster-out estimates remained negative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sports-major background was associated with shorter simple reaction time conditional on the measured covariates, although uncertain covariate timing and unmeasured cluster-level differences limit interpretation. The findings describe a group-level association and do not establish neural mechanisms or the usefulness of this measure for individual monitoring or screening.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association between sports-major background and simple reaction time in physically active university students: a cross-sectional study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We establish quintet mixed-reference spin-flip response with a dressed kernel (QMRSF-DK), an extension of MRSF-TDDFT for systems with four strongly correlated orbitals. The central ingredient is to use ten reference determinants constructed from a common quintet restricted open-shell Kohn–Sham (ROKS) orbital set. The eight complementary Ms = ±1 reference determinants (Ξr(±1)) generate the 30 open-shell Ms = 0 response configurations through single-spin-flip linear response, whereas the Ms = ±2 pair (Ξ(±2)) provides the energy origin and supplies exactly the six missing closed-shell Ms = 0 configurations through a selective dressed kernel. Together, these 36 response configurations span the complete spin-adapted active space of four electrons in four orbitals [CAS(4,4)], comprising 20 singlets, 15 triplets, and one quintet. The expanded four-orbital space restores the complete 3P and 1P degeneracies of Be. For H4, it describes the potential-energy profiles of the three lowest strongly correlated singlets along the square-to-rectangle distortion. For ethylene, it recovers the double-bond-breaking potential-energy surfaces of the C═C bond, including the correct spin-degenerate separated-fragment limit. For polyene dimers, it reproduces XMS-CASPT2(4,4) with a mean absolute error of 0.198 eV over 24 character-matched states, including the singlet-coupled triplet-pair state, 1(TT). Collectively, these results establish a foundation for extending the MRSF-TDDFT framework to substantially larger strongly correlated systems.</jats:p>

                    A simultaneous spectroscopic and visualization system was developed to study hypersonic shock layer radiation along a streamwise line-of-sight (LOS). The system was implemented to observe emissions ahead of a projectile traveling at approximately 7 km s

Experimental conditions were designed to establish equilibrium flow within the shock layer, enabling comparison of the measured emission spectra with equilibrium radiation models. Radiation calculations were performed using the SPRADIAN07 radiation code, with equilibrium flow properties obtained using the NASA CEA code. The dominant thermochemical structure in the shock layer was analyzed by streamlining the radiative transfer within a piecewise layer model. Parameterized layer properties were iteratively refined until the calculated spectra matched the experimental spectra. The findings demonstrate that the current measurement method provides useful diagnostic information for estimating the dissociating, partially ionizing, and ablating structure of hypersonic shock layers in addition to reducing uncertainty associated with LOS measurements.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Redox chemistry of L - cysteine is important in biological systems, pharmaceutical chemistry, environmental chemistry and chemical research. This importance arises mainly from the presence of thiol group in its molecular structure, which enables L - cysteine to participate in redox reactions. The kinetics and mechanism of the redox reaction of safranin - O with L – cysteine (LSH) have been investigated spectrophotometrically in aqueous acidic medium under the following conditions: [H+] = 2.0 × 10-5 mol dm-3, I = 0.3 C2 mol dm-3 (NaCl), ʎmax = 520 nm and T = 294 ± 1K. The aim of this study is to investigate the kinetics of the reaction of safranin - O with L - cysteine in aqueous acidic solution. The reaction was monitored at 520 nm under pseudo first order conditions by following the decrease in absorbance of the dye with time.  The reaction was first order in both [SO+] and [LSH], with second order overall. Studies on the effect of hydrogen ion concentration revealed the participation of a deprotonated reactive species prior to electron transfer. Negative BrØnsted Debye salt effect was observed, suggesting participation of oppositely charged reacting species in the rate determining step. Spectroscopic investigation gave no evidence for the formation of an intermediate complex of significant stability in the reaction. Free radicals were not detected during the course of the reaction. items.abstract: <jats:p>Advancing Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF), particularly Fast Ignition and Shock Ignition, requires a deeper understanding of laser–plasma interactions in extreme regimes that remain difficult to access at large-scale ICF facilities. Long-wave infrared (LWIR) lasers provide a powerful approach, leveraging favorable wavelength scaling to access relativistic plasma physics, enable efficient laser beam channeling, and enhance the generation of hot electrons and energetic ions at significantly reduced laser intensity and plasma density. This capability allows laboratory-scale experiments to reproduce ICF-relevant conditions with improved diagnostic access and greater physical transparency. The Brookhaven National Laboratory Accelerator Test Facility offers a unique platform for such studies, combining a multi-terawatt LWIR laser with synchronized optical diagnostics and accelerator-based probes. This capability enables systematic investigation and optimization of key plasma processes governing ICF performance, thereby supporting the development of practical fusion energy systems.</jats:p>
title: Long wave infrared laser platform for plasma studies relevant to inertial fusion

items.abstract: <jats:p>Configuring a diagnostic before the next shot is an instrumentation problem that grows in importance as high-repetition-rate laser-plasma platforms scale from tens of shots to thousands. In the present campaign, a gated intensified optical camera required shot-to-shot retuning as peak image brightness varied with chamber pressure, laser energy, focus conditions, and target state. Static settings produced under-exposed or over-driven images, while manual tuning consumed shots and reduced measurement efficiency. We treat this problem as machine-learning-guided pre-shot diagnostic configuration using a hybrid framework: archived images and machine variables are reduced to a compact descriptor state, a neural-network surrogate is trained to predict that state from operating conditions and detector settings, and Bayesian optimization inverts the surrogate to recommend executable settings before each shot. On a 1 Hz multi-joule platform, the measured peak signal tracked requested targets from 1000 to 4500 counts with a correlation of 0.92 and a mean absolute error of 15%. These results demonstrate that campaign data can train practical empirical models supporting pre-shot diagnostic configuration for enhanced data quality and experimental efficiency in comparable laser-plasma campaigns.</jats:p>
title: Machine-learning-guided pre-shot diagnostic configuration for high-repetition-rate laser-plasma experiments

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>New experimental densities are reported for n-hexane (1) + soybean oil biodiesel (2) mixtures, measured with a calibrated Anton Paar DMA-HPM densimeter at 298.15–393.15 K and 0.1–140 MPa over the full composition range, giving 768 new state points. The Tait equation correlates every composition within 0.006–0.10% AAD and was used to derive the isobaric thermal expansivity (αp = (6.15–13.29) × 10–4 K–1) and isothermal compressibility (κT = (4.37–23.58) × 10–4 MPa–1) of the mixture. A classical Perturbed-Chain SAFT (PC-SAFT) model was applied, with pure-component parameters regressed on the hexane and biodiesel data and a single binary interaction parameter, k12, regressed as a quadratic function of composition, k12(x1). This composition-dependent model reaches an overall AAD of 0.51% (0.19–0.89% by composition), a nearly 3-fold improvement over the AAD of 1.60% obtained when k12 is instead held constant across composition. A hybrid PC-SAFT-ANN model, correcting the PC-SAFT residual with a compact neural network and evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation on data never seen during training, reduces the AAD to 0.013% overall (0.0095–0.021% by composition), a near two-orders-of-magnitude improvement over PC-SAFT alone. This hybrid strategy recovers essentially all of the missing physical accuracy without the large multicompound training databases that genuine graph neural networks require, offering a practical, honestly validated alternative for binary systems with limited experimental data.</jats:p>
title: High-Pressure, High-Temperature Density of n -Hexane + Soybean Oil Biodiesel Binary Mixtures: New Experimental Data and a Hybrid PC-SAFT-ANN Equation of State

items.abstract: <jats:p>Engine cranking draws several hundred amperes from a vehicle's 24 V storage system within fractions of a second. For lithium-ion batteries, the binding constraint under such pulses is the continuous discharge-current limit rather than the stored energy. This paper presents an experimentally parameterized simulation study of a passive hybrid energy storage system for heavy-vehicle engine starting, in which a lithium-ion battery and a supercapacitor module are connected in parallel without a DC/DC converter. An ASPİLSAN INR18650A28 cell and a Skeleton SCH3400 supercapacitor cell were characterized. A two-RC Thevenin model was identified from pulse tests at nine states of charge (RMSE 0.139–0.206 mV) and checked against an independent constant-current test, and a three-branch Zubieta–Bonert model from constant-current charge and self-discharge tests. A 7s72p battery (26.19 V, 200.6 Ah, 30.28 kg) and a ten-cell supercapacitor module (340 F, 5.65 kg) were modeled in MATLAB/Simulink under a measured five-phase cranking profile with a 1010 A peak. The supercapacitor reduced the battery peak current from 1010 to 587.7 A (5.035 to 2.930 C per cell) and the bus-voltage drop by 41.2%. Because the series–parallel configuration reverses the element-level resistance advantage of the supercapacitor, the current split is set by pack configuration and agrees within 0.8 percentage points with a resistive-divider estimate. Under the 14.0 A cell current limit, the deliverable peak power increased from 25.72 to 44.02 kW and the power density from 850 to 1225 W/kg, for an 18.7% mass increase and a 15.1% reduction in energy density.</jats:p>
title: Enhancing power density: A simulation study of passive hybrid energy storage systems for heavy vehicles

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Plasma cathodes often exhibit a bi-modal current–voltage behavior whose physical origin remains unclear, where a low voltage, low current regime transitions to a higher current, high voltage regime at some transition point. Here, two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations using EDIPIC-2D are used to study an argon electron-cyclotron-resonance plasma cathode with an extracting anode, with the goal of identifying the kinetic mechanism connecting this transition point to the formation of a confined orifice plasma. The simulations reveal two self-consistent regimes: a low-current, diffusion dominated state in which the supply of electrons to the orifice is limited, and a high-current state characterized by a dense orifice plasma separated from the prescribed discharge plasma by a weak electrostatic double layer. In the latter regime, the double layer sustains intense localized ionization by accelerating source electrons while regulating particle exchange across the interface. Ion-acoustic wave activity is observed, and a low-Mach-number ion-acoustic shock forms within the double-layer region that produces a pronounced reversal in axial ion current density immediately below this interface. Time-resolved diagnostics reveal the formation mechanism for this orifice plasma that culminates in the coupling of the source, orifice, and plume regions. These results reveal a kinetic, time-dependent mechanism for the bi-modal transition in plasma cathodes and identify electron supply, plume-ionization seeding, and double-layer-shock dynamics as key elements governing access to the high-current regime.</jats:p>
title: A kinetic simulation of orifice plasma formation in plasma cathodes

items.abstract: <jats:p>Whether psychosocial resources equitably buffer the harms of discrimination is a foundational but contested question in minority aging research, one that existing evidence from Western contexts answers inconsistently. We address this question in a structurally distinct setting: Hong Kong, a high-density, Chinese-majority global hub where South Asian and other ethnic minority residents age as post-migration minorities under compounding institutional exclusions. Drawing on the Hong Kong Elder Well-being Survey and employing propensity score matching alongside instrumental variables regression, we show that perceived discrimination is robustly associated with higher levels of depression, anxiety, loneliness and lower subjective well-being among older ethnic minorities. The critical finding is not the harm itself but its structural conditionality: low-SES elders experience stronger adverse associations between discrimination and psychological well-being while simultaneously possessing significantly lower baseline endowments of ethnic identity and sense of community. This double burden challenges two common assumptions in minority aging and active aging policy: that psychosocial resilience resources are equally accessible, and that economic integration translates into social inclusion. In stratified urban Asian societies, addressing structural racism and enabling equitable access to social infrastructure are prerequisites for, not complements to, individual-level resilience interventions.</jats:p>
title: When Resources Cannot Protect: Discrimination, Structural Constraint, and the Well-Being of Ethnic Minority Elders in a High-Density Asian City

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper develops a family of efficient numerical schemes for the non-isothermal variable density incompressible Navier-Stokes equations (VDNSEs), a representative multiphysics coupling system that poses significant challenges due to the coexistence of time derivative terms, nonlinear convection terms, the gravity and buoyancy effects. The proposed schemes are linear, fully decoupled, mass conservation and unconditional energy dissipation, achieving first and second order temporal accuracy via the Euler and BDF2 schemes, respectively. The key novelty is the introduction of two $energy-contribution$ $auxiliary$ $variables$ (ECAV) $R$ and $S$, which can treat the difficulties caused by the time derivative terms conveniently and ensure the mass conservation naturally. Combining with other auxiliary variables handle the gravity term and nonlinear terms, an equivalent system of the nonisothermal VDNSEs is reformulated. Using the pressure correction projection method to split the velocity and pressure, the linear and auxiliary terms are treated implicitly, while the nonlinear terms are approximated explicitly, two time-marching fully decoupled schemes (first order Euler and second order BDF2) are constructed. We rigorously prove discrete mass conservation, unconditional energy dissipation and the unique solvability of the numerical solutions for both schemes. Both schemes decompose the original nonlinear multi-variables coupled system into a series of linear univariate subproblems per time step, significantly reducing the computational size and complexity. Extensive numerical tests confirm the expected convergence rates, mass conservation and energy dissipation. To demonstrate robustness of the proposed numerical schemes in challenging scenarios, we simulate the Rayleigh-Bénard convection and the thermally driven cavity problem, benchmarks known for complex buoyancy-driven dynamics with strong thermal coupling, where the schemes maintain excellent stability and physical fidelity.</jats:p>
title: Mass-Conserving, Unconditionally Energy Dissipative and Fully Decoupled Schemes for Nonisothermal Variable Density Incompressible Navier-Stokes Equations

                    In this work, we investigate how electric potential and precipitation influence the storm‐time thermosphere net energy budget and subsequently neutral mass density variations during the 2023 April geomagnetic storm by using different combinations of high‐latitude forcings to drive the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM), including the Weimer convection, default statistical auroral precipitation, and the assimilative mapping of ionospheric electrodynamics (AMIE) outputs of both. Meanwhile, the realistic observations are used to validate across different simulations. We found that electric potential dominates the magnitude and pattern of density variations, whereas precipitation regulates the magnitude. Compared with Weimer, the simulations using the AMIE electric potential show better agreement with the observations, which also corresponds to a more realistic energy balance between Joule heating and NO cooling processes. Diagnostic analysis of the energy equation further shows that Joule heating and radiative cooling contribute to thermodynamic changes in the lower thermosphere. They mainly interact with adiabatic and advection processes, further leading to differences in magnitude and pattern among different simulations. Specifically, at high latitudes, the enhanced Joule heating offsets cooling due to adiabatic and advection processes, and radiative infrared emission. In contrast, at mid‐ and low‐latitudes, radiative cooling reinforces/counteracts the cooling/heating associated with adiabatic and advection processes. In addition, the observed CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    cooling also exhibits an enhanced response, indicating its contribution to the effects of radiative cooling on the energy equation. However, the TIEGCM is inadequate to represent such effect. Further investigation by the whole atmosphere model is needed.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) presents turbulence regimes that diverge from the classical Kolmogorov 1941 (K41) power-law spectrum widely assumed in optical atmospheric profiling, yet turbulence characterization for astronomical applications remains predominantly based on K41 assumptions. Using high-frequency sonic anemometer data from site-testing campaigns at the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) and Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) sites in Chile, we apply detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA)—a technique from fractal time-series analysis—to identify the inertial sub-range and evaluate statistical isotropy in the ABL, comparing our approach with the Fourier-based algorithm for robust identification of the inertial subrange (ARIIS). Strict Kolmogorov conditions—simultaneous isotropy and k−5/3 scaling across all fields—are satisfied in fewer than 7 per cent of observations. Temperature fields systematically decouple from velocity components under stable stratification, exhibiting Bolgiano-Obukhov scaling (k−7/5) during nighttime hours, indicating active rather than passive scalar behaviour. DFA-detected regime transitions correlate with characteristic turbulence scales, providing objective, model-free boundaries for the inertial subrange. Comparative $C_n^2$ estimation reveals that structure function methods assuming K41 scaling diverge significantly from flux-based parameterizations under stable conditions. The rarity of true Kolmogorov conditions at these sites necessitates stratification-aware methodologies for accurate optical turbulence characterization at next-generation extremely large telescope facilities.</jats:p>
title: Inertial sub-range detection and characterization for ground-layer turbulence at new extremely large telescope sites in Chile

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fusion and fragmentation are intrinsic dynamic pathways in block copolymer micelles, governing both structural transformations and the transport of solubilized molecules. Yet, how the macromolecular architecture controls their energetic barriers remains poorly understood. In particular, while the influence of the core-forming block has been investigated, the contribution of the corona remains less explored, especially for fusion under equilibrium conditions. Here, this contribution is examined by quantifying equilibrium fusion and fragmentation kinetics in aqueous Pluronic PEO–PPO–PEO micelles from the time-resolved intermicellar exchange of an extremely hydrophobic fluorescent probe. A systematic series of copolymers with comparable PPO block lengths and PEO blocks spanning approximately 17–140 EO units was examined in the spherical-micelle regime and combined with previously reported data for copolymers spanning a broader range of PPO block lengths. Increasing the corona length produces only weak changes in both fusion and fragmentation rates, in marked contrast to the much stronger dependence on core length. The apparent activation energies for fusion and fragmentation are remarkably similar in magnitude and exhibit closely related dependences on block architecture. For both processes, this dependence is described by a common scaling form, ΔEapp ∝ NcoreaNcoronab, with a ≈ 1.3–2 and b close to zero. These results demonstrate that the energetic cost of equilibrium fusion and fragmentation is governed predominantly by the micellar core.</jats:p>
title: Corona-Length Dependence of Equilibrium Fusion and Fragmentation Energy Barriers in Block Copolymer Micelles

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper proposes a coordinated configuration method for reactive power compensation using capacitor banks and static var generators (SVGs) to address frequent changes in power-flow direction and reactive demand on the low-voltage side of substations caused by high-proportion distributed photovoltaic (PV) integration. First, an equivalent substation model with distributed PV is developed, and six representative operating scenarios are constructed to account for seasonal, weather, and load variations. The optimal reactive compensation requirement is then determined under voltage and power-factor constraints. Next, a two-layer capacitor-SVG compensation architecture is proposed, in which capacitor banks provide slowly varying capacitive compensation via hourly switching, while SVGs compensate for switching discretization errors, residual intra-hour fluctuations, and inductive demand when absorption is needed. A life-cycle cost model is established considering five components: initial investment, operating losses, maintenance, replacement, and salvage value. A planned 110/10.5 kV substation is used as a case study. The influence of inverter reactive power control, including constant power factor, constant reactive power, and Volt/Var, on the compensation requirements, equipment configuration, and life-cycle cost is also evaluated. Results show that, under voltage and power-factor constraints, a configuration of twelve 1.8 MVar capacitor groups and two 8 MVar SVGs achieves the lowest life-cycle cost. Sensitivity analysis indicates that SVG unit cost and discount rate are the dominant economic factors.</jats:p>
title: Coordinated capacitor-SVG reactive power compensation configuration for substations with high-penetration distributed photovoltaic integration
