                    In this study, 304, 316L, and 316LN austenitic stainless steels were subjected to neutron irradiation at a relatively low fluence of 1 × 10
                    <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                     n/cm
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    , and their tensile properties were evaluated before and after irradiation. Notably, the ductility of 316L and 316LN steels increased by more than 25% without a significant reduction in ultimate tensile strength, whereas both ductility and strength of 304 stainless steel remained essentially unchanged. Neutron irradiation introduces point defects that subsequently evolve into a complex defect network consisting of dislocations, stacking faults, and deformation. The resulting strain fields exhibit pronounced spatial heterogeneity, forming chain‐like and banded distributions along dislocation lines, stacking‐fault arrays, and twin interfaces, indicative of strong local strain gradients and stress concentration effects. The incorporation of twin boundaries, stacking faults, and multioriented domains provides additional deformation accommodation pathways, including twinning‐induced plasticity (TWIP) and interface‐mediated slip, while simultaneously promoting sustained dislocation nucleation and glide. These mechanisms facilitate progressive strain delocalization across heterogeneous microstructural units, effectively suppress strain localization, and thereby enhance overall ductility. These findings provide a design strategy for irradiation‐tolerant alloys that retain high strength while achieving enhanced ductility under neutron exposure in next‐generation nuclear systems.
                  </jats:p>
title: Low‐Fluence Neutron Irradiation Slightly Enhances the Ductility of 316L and 316LN Austenitic Stainless Steels

items.abstract: <jats:p>Rapid identification of likely transport directions and particle deposition zones is needed after a nuclear accident, particularly before a defensible radionuclide source term and field network are available. We conducted a retrospective Fukushima case study to test the information content of a daily GOCI constrained PM2.5 series used to weight particle releases from the known plant location. The archived calculation released 7,163,349 computational particles from March 11 through March 30, 2011 and transported them with hourly winds, terrain dependent stochastic spreading, empirical dry removal, and precipitation dependent wet scavenging on a 0.05° grid. The plant PM2.5 series showed weak and nonsignificant daily correspondence with the monitoring constrained reverse estimates of iodine 131 and cesium 137 release from Katata et al. Pearson correlations were 0.275 and 0.255. These source terms were reconstructed after the accident from environmental observations and dispersion calculations. They were not direct measurements of emissions. No independent accident period radionuclide monitoring station was available within the modeled study area. The spatial analysis therefore compares March relative deposition with a later June and July air dose field and uses the Meteorological Research Institute site, about 172 km southwest of the plant, only as external temporal context. After georegistration to 1,050 common cells, modeled relative deposition and the later air dose field had Pearson’s r of 0.511 with a spatial block bootstrap 95 percent interval from 0.334 to 0.729. Spearman’s rho was 0.462 and bivariate Moran’s I was 0.494 with a fixed seed permutation p value of 0.0001. The model recovered 65.2 percent of the highest 20 percent of air dose cells. Particle number experiments were stable, but uniform hourly source weighting produced an almost identical map with a correlation of 0.9986 to the PM2.5 weighted baseline. Nearly all particles occupied the smallest numerical size class. The broad spatial agreement is therefore attributable mainly to the known source location, wind sequence, and empirical removal rather than evidence that the PM2.5 series reproduced radionuclide release timing. The transported population may include newly condensed accident particles and ambient particles that acquired radionuclides, but its radioactive fraction is unknown. The method may support rapid directional screening for particle associated contamination, but it does not estimate radionuclide activity, gas transport, dose, or exposure.</jats:p>
title: Rapid screening of particle associated deposition after a nuclear accident using satellite constrained aerosol weighting

items.abstract: <jats:p>Scientific theories of consciousness (STOCs) routinely claim, in one form or another, that consciousness does something: that it confers a function and a behavioral or adaptive advantage. This paper asks what that claim can coherently amount to. A conceptual analysis of the four leading STOCs—global workspace, higher-order, integrated information, and recurrent processing theories—shows that beneath their well-known disagreements they share four commitments: every conscious state has a minimally sufficient neural correlate (neural sufficiency); consciousness confers a functional gain (functional efficacy); neural and biological states supervene on physical states (supervenience); and that the physical domain forms a causally complete system (causal self-sufficiency). Held together, these commitments generate a specific difficulty. Although they do not exclude higher-level causation, they constrain the attribution of an additional behavioral difference to phenomenal experience over and above the difference already made by its sufficient physical realizer. On this basis the paper identifies a functional fallacy: inferring a function of phenomenal experience from evidence that establishes only a function of its neural realizer or of associated access mechanisms. To diagnose and avoid the fallacy, the paper develops a diagnostic framework that specifies the target, causal evidence, and explanatory level of functional attributions, together with an evidential ladder distinguishing weak, medium, and strong functional claims. Applying the framework to functional explanation and to empirical paradigms shows how it supports the precise operationalization of conscious experience, disciplines the interpretation of experiments, and facilitates theory comparison in psychological science.</jats:p>
title: The functional fallacy: a diagnostic framework for functional claims in the psychology of consciousness

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case overview/synopsis</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Banas Dairy was Asia’s largest dairy cooperative. It transported liquid milk from its Palanpur plant, Gujarat to Faridabad plant, Delhi National Capital Region. For this transportation, Banas dairy used railway milk tankers (RMTs) and road transport. These modes inherently had some concerns. For example, in RMTs there were frequent delays, repetitive milk transfers and increased costs due to demurrage charged by Indian Railways (IR). Along with that, another grave issue was maintaining the quality of milk. In trucking mode, truck drivers had to undergo risks of pilferage, road accidents and police harassment. In 2021, the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited (DFCCIL) offered the ToT service on its Western Dedicated Corridor of India (The Economic Times, 2025a). Part A of this case was positioned around six months before the Banas Dairy actually adopted the ToT. That time, conundrum was whether Banas Dairy would change its transportation mode to the ToT. The conundrum faced by Banas Dairy would have to be resolved under the able guidance of Mr Sangram R. Chaudhary, managing director of Banas Dairy. The change was to be implemented in the immediate future to overcome the cons posed by the RMTs and road transport. Part B of this case, which was based on 2023–2026 and covered the period after the shift to ToT mode, showed another dilemma – how to optimize the return journey of the ToT. This case study detailed the operations of the DFCCIL and the salient features of the ToT. It highlighted logistics improvements, savings in fuel costs and the positive environmental effects of innovative logistics, especially in rail transport, in a developing economy such as India. This is a teaching note supplementing the “Neither truck nor train, rather truck on train: innovative freight fusion or patchwork?” case study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Complexity academic level</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case study is designed for undergraduate or graduate-level programs in supply chain and logistics or strategy management, and senior management professionals in executive education programs undertaking courses in logistics management, supply chain operations and related cargo logistics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Subject code</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CSS 9: Operations and Logistics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Neither truck nor train, rather truck on train: innovative freight fusion or patchwork?

<jats:title>Abstract:</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Collision tumors (CTs) are lesions in which 2 histologically distinct neoplasms of different cellular lineages arise in proximity within a single lesion while maintaining a demarcated interface. CTs combining a keratinocytic malignancy with melanoma are uncommon, and those containing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) rather than basal cell carcinoma (BCC) are even rarer. Melanoma in situ (MIS) as the melanocytic partner is likewise an uncommon finding. We report a 78-year-old man with a CT composed of SCC and MIS. This case illustrates the diagnostic pitfalls posed by 1 component obscuring the other amid background inflammation, the importance of proper histologic classification, and the value of immunohistochemical studies in guiding appropriate management.</jats:p>
title: Squamomelanocytic Collision Tumor of the Chest: A Diagnostic Pitfall in Sun-Damaged Skin

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose of review</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC)﻿ is an aggressive cutaneous malignancy for which immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)﻿ have significantly improved clinical outcomes. However, approximately half of patients do not respond to ICIs, and recurrence rates remain high. This review summarizes the latest clinical evidence on diagnostic and predictive biomarkers, as well as emerging therapeutic strategies, aiming to improve clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Recent findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Several studies have highlighted the potential of immune cell subsets, including myeloid cells and T cells, as prognostic and predictive biomarkers in MCC. For clinical surveillance, circulating tumor DNA has emerged as a promising tool and is included in the NCCN guideline recommendations for follow-up. Regarding emerging therapeutic strategies, ICI monotherapy remains the standard first-line treatment for unresectable or metastatic MCC. Although neoadjuvant and adjuvant immunotherapy strategies have shown promising results in terms of pathological response and recurrence reduction, respectively, an overall survival benefit has not yet been established. Finally, ICI discontinuation may be considered in selected patients who achieve a complete response and have received at least one year of treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this review, we focused on the latest literature regarding emerging biomarkers, the role of circulating tumor DNA in clinical surveillance, and novel therapeutic strategies, with particular emphasis on adjuvant, neoadjuvant, and multimodal approaches in MCC. We also reviewed new evidence aimed at establishing the optimal treatment duration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Emerging diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in the management of Merkel cell carcinoma

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to develop preliminary validity evidence for the Scale for Autism in Females (SAF), a semi-structured diagnostic interview designed to capture the often-overlooked presentation of autism in girls. For decades, autism assessment has been shaped primarily by male-centered diagnostic frameworks, contributing to the under-recognition of many females. Using a Delphi-style expert review process, experienced clinicians evaluated the SAF across three rounds of review. Findings provided initial evidence of face and content validity and informed revisions to strengthen the scale. As an early-stage instrument, the SAF represents a first step toward more inclusive, gender informed assessment practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study used a qualitative Delphi-style design to support the initial development and preliminary validation of the SAF, a clinician-guided semi-structured diagnostic interview designed to assess the female autism phenotype. Twenty-eight experienced clinicians with expertise in autism diagnosis participated in 3 rounds of structured expert review. Using the Content Analysis and Evaluation Protocol rubric, participants evaluated each item’s clarity, representativeness, importance and utility while also providing feedback. Quantitative ratings were analyzed and thematic analysis of written responses guided iterative revisions to strengthen the SAF’s face and content validity and clinical applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings provided strong preliminary evidence of the SAF’s face and content validity. Across three rounds of expert review, clinicians consistently rated SAF items highly in clarity, representativeness, importance and clinical utility, with all items ultimately exceeding the established consensus threshold. Qualitative thematic analysis identified five major themes that informed iterative revisions to the measure, including differentiation from neurotypicality, level of insight, gender and sexuality considerations, clinician training gaps and formatting improvements. Feedback led to revisions that strengthened the scale’s accessibility, organization and clinical relevance. Overall, results supported the SAF as a promising early-stage tool for identifying the female autism phenotype.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight the growing need for assessments that recognize the experiences of autistic women rather than relying primarily on male-centered diagnostic frameworks. The SAF offers clinicians a structured way to explore camouflaging, internalized social difficulties and relational patterns that contribute to delayed or missed diagnosis. The study also underscores ongoing gaps in clinician training surrounding the female autism phenotype. However, the SAF remains an early-stage instrument. Limitations include a relatively small and demographically homogeneous expert sample and the absence of direct validation from autistic females. Future research should include psychometric validation, normative data, factor analysis and clinical comparison studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The SAF represents an early but important step toward more inclusive and gender informed autism assessment practices and, to our knowledge, is the first diagnostic interview developed with the female autism phenotype at the core of its conceptualization. By exploring experiences such as masking, social exhaustion and compensatory coping strategies, the SAF expands beyond the externally observable behaviors emphasized in traditional assessments. Although further psychometric validation is needed, the SAF may support earlier identification and more affirming diagnostic experiences in clinical, school, outpatient and multidisciplinary assessment settings while increasing clinician awareness of subtle female autism presentations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The SAF has important social implications for autistic women who have historically been overlooked, misunderstood or diagnosed later in life due to male-centered diagnostic frameworks. More accurate recognition of autism improves access to educational supports, mental health services and community resources while reducing experiences of isolation and chronic masking. Diagnoses also affect not only the individual, but their families, educators, peers and support systems by increasing understanding and helping others respond with greater empathy. Although still in the early stages of development, the SAF represents a step toward more inclusive diagnostic practices that better reflect the diversity of autistic experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the SAF is the first clinician-guided diagnostic interview developed with women at the center of its conceptualization rather than treating female presentations as secondary to male-centered diagnostic frameworks. This study contributes an early but meaningful step toward addressing the long-standing underrecognition of autistic women in research and clinical practice. By centering experiences of compensatory coping strategies, the SAF seeks to amplify presentations that have historically been overlooked or misunderstood. Beyond assessment, the SAF may also serve as a clinician training framework that encourages more inclusive, affirming and equitable approaches to autism identification across settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Scale for autism in females (SAF): a diagnostic interview for the female phenotype

items.abstract: <jats:p>Objectives. Epilepsy occurs far more often in autistic people than in the general population, contributing to drug resistance, hospitalization and reduced quality of life, yet seizures are both under-recognized and over-diagnosed. This review examines the epidemiology, neurobiology, diagnostic pitfalls and management of epilepsy in autism. Material and methods. A structured literature search for a narrative review was undertaken in PubMed/MEDLINE, supplemented by targeted identification of International League Against Epilepsy position statements, covering literature to July 2026 with emphasis on publications from 2021 onwards. Original studies published in full were prioritized, alongside systematic reviews, meta-analyses and consensus statements; no systematic-review methodology was applied. Results. Pooled prevalence is approximately 10% (95% CI 6–14%), although estimates are heterogeneous, with risk concentrated in intellectual disability, limited language, regression and genetic syndromes. The conditions converge on synaptic, ion-channel and excitation–inhibition mechanisms. Nonepileptic staring, stereotypies and sleep-related events obscure recognition. Interictal epileptiform discharges are frequent and of uncertain significance, and an abnormal electroencephalogram alone does not establish epilepsy. Genetic diagnostic yield is higher in several overlapping neurodevelopmental comorbidity subgroups, though evidence specific to the combined co-occurrence of autism, epilepsy and intellectual disability is limited. Retrospective series show meaningful seizure benefit in selected surgical candidates; short-term hospital safety and utilization outcomes appear similar between autistic and non-autistic patients, but comparative evidence on long-term seizure outcomes remains limited. Conclusions. Diagnosis and management should be individualized, evidence-informed and multidisciplinary; autism alone should not restrict access to full epilepsy evaluation or treatment.</jats:p>
title: Epilepsy in autism spectrum disorder: shared neurobiology, diagnostic challenges, and evidence-informed clinical management

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate whether lesion conspicuity remains consistent between diagnostic and biopsy acquisitions in recombined-only lesions undergoing contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM)-guided biopsy, and to identify determinants of reduced procedural conspicuity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective single-centre study included 169 consecutive recombined-only lesions undergoing CEM-guided biopsy between October 2019 and September 2025. Lesion conspicuity (LC) was assessed on diagnostic and projection-matched stereotactic scout recombined images using a three-level ordinal scale (low, moderate, or high). Reduced procedural conspicuity was defined as a decrease in LC category. Continuous perceptual variation was assessed using a visual analogue scale (VAS). Associations between ordinal LC change (ΔLC) and median VAS were evaluated using Spearman correlation. Multivariable logistic regression using Firth’s penalized likelihood method was performed to identify predictors of reduced conspicuity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Procedural LC was maintained or increased in 136/169 lesions (80.5%), whereas reduced conspicuity occurred in 33/169 lesions (19.5%). The same diagnostic and procedural LC category was observed in 111/169 lesions (65.7%). ΔLC correlated with median VAS (Spearman ρ = 0.665;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, non-mass enhancement morphology (adjusted OR 5.10, 95% CI: 1.94–14.06;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) was independently associated with reduced conspicuity, whereas marked background parenchymal enhancement demonstrated a positive but statistically non-significant trend (adjusted OR 3.49, 95% CI: 0.97–12.55;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.055). Technical variables were not independently associated.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LC remained largely consistent between diagnostic and procedural acquisitions in most lesions undergoing CEM-guided biopsy. Reduced conspicuity was primarily associated with non-mass enhancement morphology rather than acquisition-related factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Key Points</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:bold>
                        <jats:italic>Question</jats:italic>
                      </jats:bold>
                      <jats:italic>Does LC remain consistent between diagnostic and biopsy acquisitions during CEM-guided biopsy, and which factors are associated with reduced procedural conspicuity?</jats:italic>
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:bold>
                        <jats:italic>Findings</jats:italic>
                      </jats:bold>
                      <jats:italic>LC remained stable or increased in most lesions undergoing CEM-guided biopsy, with reduced conspicuity primarily associated with non-mass enhancement morphology</jats:italic>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:bold>
                        <jats:italic>Clinical relevance</jats:italic>
                      </jats:bold>
                      <jats:italic>LC is generally preserved at the CEM-guided biopsy scout acquisition, supporting consistent procedural visualisation of recombined-only lesions</jats:italic>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Consistency of diagnostic-to-procedural lesion conspicuity in contrast-enhanced mammography-guided biopsy
